title: Food Words: Countable and Uncountable, Some and Any
summary: Learn how to talk about food using countable and uncountable nouns. Discover when to use 'some' and 'any' correctly.

sections.p: Countable nouns are things we can count with numbers. We can use 'a' or 'an' before them in the singular. They also have a plural form with an 's' at the end, like apples or bananas. You can ask 'How many?' for these words.

ex.en: I have an apple in my bag.
ex.mean: One apple that you can count.
Asking about a specific number of bananas.

ex.en: We need to buy some carrots.
ex.mean: More than one carrot, in a plural form.

sections.p: Uncountable nouns are things we cannot count with numbers. They do not have a plural form, so we never say 's' at the end. We cannot use 'a' or 'an' with them. You can ask 'How much?' for these words, like water, milk, or rice.

ex.en: Can I have some milk, please?
ex.mean: Asking for an uncountable amount of liquid.

ex.en: There is no rice left in the kitchen.
ex.mean: Rice is a substance you do not count one by one.

sections.p: We use 'some' in positive sentences for both countable and uncountable nouns when we have an amount. We use 'any' in negative sentences with 'not' and in questions. 'Any' means zero or we are asking if something exists.

ex.en: I have some bread for breakfast.
ex.mean: Positive sentence with an uncountable noun.

ex.en: We do not have any apples.

tip: Remember: if you can put a number like 'one' or 'two' directly in front of the noun, it is countable. If it sounds strange, it is probably uncountable!

quiz.en: Do we have ___ milk in the fridge?
Is there ___ coffee in the cup?
